operator_io_quirks: All identifiers are mixed-case (Customers, Customer_Policies, Policy_Type_Code, Date_Claim_Made); must be double-quoted with original spelling in generated SQL.
Tiny DB: every table has exactly 15 rows; original_values lists are short (<=15), so rng.choices(k=min(5,len)) draws heavily from a handful of values.
DATE columns are declared DATE but stored as TEXT 'YYYY-MM-DD' (e.g. '2018-01-21'); storage class contradicts declared type.
DATE columns dispatch to 'Date|Number(int elements)' — first element '2018-01-21' does not parse as int, so Date fuzzer with template %Y-%m-%d is chosen.
CHAR(15) Policy_Type_Code and VARCHAR(255) Payment_Method_Code are short enums (4 distinct each: Car/Life/Property/Travel; MasterCard/Discover Card/Visa/American Express).
Settlements.Customer_Policy_ID is INTEGER NOT NULL but has NO declared FK (dangling semantic reference to Customer_Policies.Policy_ID); upstream treats it as a plain Number column.
FK chain Customers -> Customer_Policies -> Claims -> Settlements -> Payments is a clean linear DAG; no self-references, no composite keys, no missing parents.
FK child columns are NOT NULL (Customer_ID, Policy_ID, Claim_ID, Settlement_ID) but upstream does not enforce NOT NULL in Python; rows violating it fail at insert and are skipped.
All PKs are single-column INTEGER NOT NULL; Number fuzzer with scale=0 gives range [-1,1] plus +-1/+-2 perturbations, so PK collisions are frequent and sample_fresh_primary_keys will drop many rows.
Amount_Claimed/Amount_Settled/Amount_Payment are INTEGER with values in the 10^3..10^6 range; Number fuzzer scale=0 will produce tiny values (near -1..1) — implausible magnitudes.
No views, triggers, or indexes beyond PKs; DDL is simple CREATE TABLE only.
null_rate is 0.0 everywhere in the original, but several columns are declared nullable (Start_Date, End_Date, Amount_*, Date_*); TS may emit NULLs via empty parent FK draws.
operator_ts_expectations: Date fuzzer with template %Y-%m-%d on all DATE columns; range from min/max of the 5 sampled originals (roughly 2016-2018), so fresh dates stay in that window — plausible.
String fuzzer on Customer_Details (VARCHAR(255)): random strings over a-zA-Z 0-9() of length 0..20 plus contaminate; will produce implausible names but that is TS behaviour.

String fuzzer on Policy_Type_Code (CHAR(15)) and Payment_Method_Code (VARCHAR(255)): length range from originals (3..7 / 4..15), so fresh strings are short but not the 4 enum values — drives FN on equality filters like Policy_Type_Code='Car'.
Number fuzzer on INTEGER columns with scale=0: full range [-1,1], list range [min(el), 1]; PKs and amounts get tiny/negative values, so Amount_Claimed > 50000 style predicates return empty — FN.

Number fuzzer on FK columns (Customer_ID, Policy_ID, Claim_ID, Settlement_ID) is bypassed: fill_foreign_keys_consistently draws from parent's final values, so FK joins are consistent — good for join queries.
Settlements.Customer_Policy_ID is a plain Number column (no FK), so it gets random tiny ints unrelated to Customer_Policies.Policy_ID — any query joining on it returns empty (FN).

PK collisions: Number scale=0 on 15-row tables with max_l0 cap often reuses fresh draws, so sample_fresh_primary_keys drops many rows; final table sizes may be much smaller than chosen (e.g. 1-5 rows).
drop_unique_duplicates on single-column PKs is redundant (PK already unique) but harmless.

Empty parent FK draws: if a parent table's PK filtering leaves 0 rows, child FK columns become NULL — but child FK columns are NOT NULL, so those rows fail at insert and are skipped, shrinking child tables.
Literal pool from train SQL will contain 'Car','Life','Property','Travel','MasterCard','Visa', etc.; String fuzzer picks these w.p. 1-p (0.8) so enum values DO appear — good for equality predicates.
Date literal pool from train SQL (e.g. '2018-01-21') feeds the Date fuzzer's element list, so template and range are anchored to real dates — plausible.

Known FP source: TS does not enforce Amount_Settled <= Amount_Claimed or Start_Date <= End_Date; queries with such predicates may return rows the original would not — but original also has no such constraint, so this is a tie/duplicate issue not a constraint issue.
